title: M44, NGC 2632
caption: The Beehive Cluster, M44, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This approximately true-color picture shows M44, the Beehive Cluster, also called Praesepe, which is Latin for manger. It is an open cluster in the constellation Cancer, and one of the nearest open clusters to us, close to 600 light-years away.
The Beehive is easy to see with the naked eye and covers a patch of sky more than twice as wide as the full Moon. Because it is so obvious, people have noticed it since prehistoric times.

When Galileo acquired his new telescope, the Beehive was among the first things he pointed it at. An open cluster like this is a loose group of stars that formed together, and being so close makes M44 a convenient place to study how such stars develop.
scale: The Beehive is close to 600 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak captured the Beehive in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-color picture.
understand.eye: The Beehive is easy to see with the naked eye, but the camera separates it into individual stars and records their colors.

explore: Fifteen images went into this picture, taken through B, V and R filters in January 1997 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope at its Warner and Swasey Observatory, on Kitt Peak near Tucson, Arizona.
alt: A wide, loose group of bright stars spread across a starry field.
